html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. LLM: large language model; BLEU: Bilingual Evaluation Understudy; ROUGE: Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation

  • How to turn requirements into measurable success criteria and metrics
  • How to build evaluation datasets
  • Mixed methodologies: code-graded, LLM-graded, human-graded
  • An evaluation framework that runs on every change

2Success Criteria and Metrics

Running case

Lumen Advisory Defines "Good" for a Bank's Claims-Triage Assistant

  • The bank says "it must be accurate, fast, cheap and safe"
  • Lumen turns each word into a number and a test

Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant. Most systems need several dimensions at once.

Dimension Example metric and target How to measure
Accuracy / task fidelity 95% correct triage category on a held-out set Exact match against labels
Faithfulness (RAG) 98% of claims supported by cited passages LLM-judge or citation check
Retrieval quality recall@20 at least 97% Labeled relevant passages
Consistency Same answer for paraphrases Similarity across paraphrase sets
Latency p95 under 3 seconds; time to first token under 1 second Timing logs
Cost Under $0.02 per case Token and price accounting
Safety Under 0.1% of outputs flagged harmful Classifier or judge on samples
Security 0 successful injection attacks in the red-team set Adversarial tests
Reliability Error and timeout rate below 0.5% Production metrics

  • Metric families: task-specific (F1, BLEU, ROUGE), generic (accuracy, precision, recall), operational (latency, uptime), safety (flag rate), qualitative scales (Likert or rubric) alongside numbers.
  • Define the threshold before you test, and which metrics are gates (must pass) versus tracked.
  • Precision and recall trade off: choose by the cost of a miss versus a false alarm (for example fraud flags).
Exam tip

"Accurate" is not a metric. The architect's answer states specific numeric criteria on a held-out dataset, across several dimensions.

3Evaluation Datasets

Source Use
Expert-written golden cases Core behavior with trusted labels
Production samples (consented, redacted) Real distribution; update regularly
Edge cases Empty, very long or irrelevant input, sarcasm, mixed signals, ambiguous items where humans disagree
Adversarial and red-team cases Prompt injection, jailbreaks, data-exfiltration attempts
Synthetic cases Scale and coverage; generated by a model and reviewed
  • Mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases.
  • Volume over polish: many automatically graded items beat a few hand-graded ones, but label quality matters; review disagreements.
  • Keep a held-out set untouched by prompt tuning to avoid overfitting to the dev set.
  • Version datasets; add every production failure as a new case (a regression set).
  • Avoid leakage: do not put eval answers in the prompt or few-shot examples.
  • Start small (about 20 representative cases) to find big problems fast, then grow.

4Mixed Methodologies

Method Strength Weakness Use for
Code-graded (exact match, regex, schema, unit checks) Fast, cheap, reliable Only for checkable answers Classification, extraction, format, tool-call correctness
LLM-graded (rubric, Likert, binary) Scales; handles nuance Needs calibration; can be biased Tone, faithfulness, completeness, helpfulness
Human-graded Highest validity Slow and costly Calibration, high-stakes review, edge cases
Semantic similarity (embeddings, ROUGE) Compares to a reference Weak on correctness Summaries, paraphrase consistency
Operational telemetry Real behavior Not about correctness Latency, cost, errors

LLM-judge practice

  • Use a detailed rubric with clear criteria; ask for reasoning first, then a score or pass/fail.
  • Prefer binary or small scales; use a different model from the generator as judge when possible.
  • Calibrate against a human-labeled sample and recheck periodically.
  • Judge outcomes, not one fixed path (agent paths vary).

5An Evaluation Framework

  1. Dataset and metrics with thresholds.
  2. Harness that runs the system (prompt version, model, parameters, retrieval config) on every case and records outputs, latency and tokens.
  3. Graders by method; store scores per case.
  4. Compare to a baseline (current production) on the same cases.
  5. Gate the release (CI): block if a gated metric regresses.
  6. Online evals after release: sampled production scoring, thumbs, correction rates.
  7. Feed back new failures into the dataset.
  • Evaluate components separately (retrieval, generation, tools) and end to end.
  • For agents, evaluate outcomes and also tool-use efficiency and safety; add human testing for what automation misses.
  • Security evals are part of the suite (injection, tool abuse); safety evals test refusals and harmful-output rates.
Exam tip

"Accurate" is not a metric: state numeric targets on a held-out dataset across several dimensions.

Exam tip

Keep a held-out set untouched by tuning, and add every production failure to the regression set.

6Exam Q&A

S1A client requires the assistant to be "accurate and fast." Which restatement is best?

  • A"Accuracy will be reviewed by the team after launch"
  • B"The assistant must beat all other assistants on the market"
  • C"The assistant should feel accurate to the people who use it and respond reasonably quickly in most situations"
  • D"At least 95 percent correct on a held-out set of 1,000 labeled cases and p95 latency under 3 seconds"
Show the answer

Answer: D. Specific, measurable criteria on a defined dataset are testable.

S2Which grading method is most appropriate for checking that extracted invoice totals match labeled values?

  • AEmbedding similarity to a sample answer
  • BAn LLM judge with a Likert scale for tone and style
  • CHuman review of every single output
  • DCode-based exact match against the labels
Show the answer

Answer: D. Checkable answers should use fast, reliable code grading.

S3An LLM judge is used to score the empathy of replies. What practice improves reliability?

  • AUse the same model and prompt that generated the reply
  • BAsk the judge for a long free-text opinion without a score
  • CUse a one-line instruction and trust the first score
  • DUse a detailed rubric, have it reason before scoring, use a different model from the generator, and calibrate against human labels
Show the answer

Answer: D. Rubrics, reasoning, a separate judge and calibration make LLM grading dependable.

S4Prompt changes keep improving the dev-set score but production quality does not improve. What is the likely cause?

  • AThe dev set is too small to compute averages, so the scores are dominated by random variation
  • BThe scoring method is too fast
  • CThe model has more parameters than needed, so it overfits to the dev set during every run
  • DOverfitting to the dev set; a held-out set that is not used for tuning should be added
Show the answer

Answer: D. Tuning against the same cases inflates scores; use a held-out set.

S5Which TWO belong in an evaluation dataset? Select TWO.

  • AThe expected answers written into the system prompt
  • BProduction-like samples that reflect the real task distribution
  • CEdge and adversarial cases such as very long input and injection attempts
  • DOnly cases that previously passed
  • EOnly easy examples so the pass rate looks high
Show the answer

Answer: B, C. Realistic production-like cases and difficult edge or adversarial cases reveal the weaknesses that a clean sample would hide.

S6A production failure is found. What should the team do with it?

  • AAdd it to the regression set so future changes are tested against it
  • BRemove it from reports as an outlier
  • CKeep it only in the incident log
  • DFix it in the prompt and forget the case, since it has been resolved and cannot recur
Show the answer

Answer: A. Every production failure becomes a permanent regression case, so later changes are tested against it before release.

S7A RAG assistant's answers sometimes include claims not in the retrieved passages. Which metric tracks this?

  • ALatency at p50
  • BTokens per minute consumed by the retrieval service during the evaluation run
  • CFaithfulness (the share of claims supported by cited passages)
  • DCache hit rate
Show the answer

Answer: C. Faithfulness measures the share of claims supported by the retrieved passages, which is exactly the grounding problem described.

S8How should fraud flags be tuned when missing fraud is far costlier than a false alarm?

  • AIgnore both and maximize accuracy on balanced data
  • BFavor precision, accepting lower recall, to keep the review queue short for the fraud analysts
  • CFavor recall, accepting lower precision, and review the extra flags
  • DRemove the threshold and flag nothing
Show the answer

Answer: C. Choose the metric trade-off by the cost of each error type.

S9Which is the best first sample size for fast feedback on a new agent system?

  • ANo dataset until launch, then collect examples from the first week of production traffic
  • B100,000 cases before any run
  • CA single demo case
  • DAbout 20 representative cases, then grow as patterns emerge
Show the answer

Answer: D. A small first sample of about twenty cases reveals large effects early, and the set can grow as patterns emerge.

S10Agent runs take different valid paths to the same result. How should they be graded?

  • ABy exact match of the sequence of tool calls against a reference run for every test case
  • BBy counting the number of tokens
  • CBy outcome and key constraints, rather than requiring one fixed sequence of steps
  • DBy the length of the final answer
Show the answer

Answer: C. Agents can take different valid paths, so grading should check the outcome and key constraints rather than one fixed sequence.

S11A team wants an eval that catches regressions before every release. What is the right mechanism?

  • AWait for user complaints and then roll back
  • BRun the dataset in CI against the candidate and gate the release on defined metrics versus the baseline
  • CRun the dataset once per year
  • DAsk reviewers to read a few outputs after each release and report anything that looks unusual to the team
Show the answer

Answer: B. Running the dataset in continuous integration and gating on metrics against the baseline protects every release from regressions.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Criteria Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant; multidimensional
Dimensions Accuracy · faithfulness · retrieval · consistency · latency · cost · safety · security
Dataset Golden, production, edge, adversarial, synthetic; dev and held-out; versioned; regression set
Methods Code (checkable) · LLM judge (nuance, calibrated) · human (calibration, high stakes)
Judge Rubric, reasoning first, different model, calibrate
Framework Dataset → run → grade → compare to baseline → gate → online → feed back
Start About 20 cases, then grow
